article.title: British Ebola patient evacuated from DR Congo arrives at London hospital
article.full_text: A British doctor who tested positive for Ebola while working in the Democratic Republic of the Congo has returned to the UK for specialist treatment. The patient, whose identity is unknown, was transported home on a medical evacuation flight, the Department of Health and Social Care said on Thursday. They are now being cared for in a specialised high-level isolation unit at the Royal Free hospital in Hampstead, north London. Dr Renu Bindra, the deputy director for all-hazards public health response at the UK Health Security Agency, said: “UKHSA and the NHS have well-established and robust infection prevention and control protocols to limit the risk of onward transmission, and the risk to the wider public remains low.” A humanitarian organisation sent the doctor to DR Congo to help in the response to the outbreak, which is the second largest on record. It is the first case involving a British national contracting Ebola in the current outbreak. The Royal Free's isolation unit has strict protocols in place to prevent the patient coming into contact with any members of the public, and all staff treating the patient are equipped with the necessary personal protective equipment alongside other measures to prevent transmission. Ebola is a highly contagious, severe and often fatal illness spread through direct contact with body fluids such as the blood or vomit of infected people, or dead bodies. The current outbreak, declared in May by DR Congo’s health ministry, has surpassed 10,000 cases and 5,000 deaths. It has spread to Kenya and Uganda in east Africa, and last month Nigeria confirmed a case in its capital, Abuja. People with the disease tend to fall ill two to 21 days after contact with an orthoebolavirus. Initial symptoms include fever, aches, pains, and fatigue, but can then progress to diarrhoea, vomiting and unexplained bleeding. There have only been four confirmed cases of the virus in the UK previously. A case in 1976 was from a laboratory needle incident, and the three others involved health workers who were responding to an outbreak in West Africa between 2014 and 2015.

article.title: ‘We are a threat to Putin’: the small Norwegian news outlet with half its staff on Russia’s wanted list
article.full_text: The official newspaper of the Russian government is an unlikely source of recognition for a European news outlet critical of Vladimir Putin and providing sanctuary to exiled Russian journalists. But in May, two days after Russia tested its new intercontinental ballistic missile system nicknamed “Satan II” by Nato, an article in Rossiyskaya Gazeta prompted celebrations in a remote newsroom in the Arctic. The story about how “leading global media” reacted to the Sarmat missile test referred to just a handful of outlets including the BBC, Reuters, the Associated Press and France 24. But among them was the Barents Observer, a small, journalist-owned online newspaper publishing in English and Russian about northern Russia and the Euro-Arctic region from a modest office in the north-eastern Norwegian town of Kirkenes. It was especially surprising given that the publication had been declared an “undesirable organisation” by the office of Russia’s prosecutor general, and half of its staff journalists are on Russia’s wanted list. Its editor, Thomas Nilsen, said: “We were listed among what the Russian government newspaper itself called ‘leading global media’. That was a very good day at the Barents Observer, because it means we had reached into the inner circle of the Kremlin.” Last week the Norwegian prime minister, Jonas Gahr Støre, and the Finnish president, Alexander Stubb, held a call with Putin, marking a rare moment of contact between the Russian president and European leaders. Afterwards, Støre said there were “big differences in views” with Putin. This certainly applies when it comes to press freedom. A few days later, the Nobel prize-winning independent Russian newspaper Novaya Gazeta was forced to close, citing intolerable pressure from authorities. A short drive from the Norway-Russia border and the only remaining legal land border crossing from Russia into the European Schengen free travel area, Kirkenes is a place where rising tensions with Moscow are felt acutely. But since the full-scale invasion of Ukraine the town has also become a refuge for Russians who have found themselves targeted by Putin’s regime – some of whom are journalists who have been hired by the Barents Observer. Recently, the journalist Denis Zagore, originally from the Russian city of Murmansk, appeared in the Russian interior ministry’s database, accused of involvement with an “undesirable” organisation and failing to comply with the legal requirements for “foreign agents”. Officials in Murmansk have filed a motion to detain Zagore in absentia. He is the third Barents Observer journalist living in exile in Kirkenes to be added to Russia’s wanted list. Despite this, like the rest of his colleagues he remains determined to continue his work unaffected. “I can’t say this came as a surprise, given that the actions of the Russian state are quite predictable and the initiation of criminal cases was only a matter of time,” he said in an interview. “I don’t intend to change anything in my life because of this. Besides, they could have found me without declaring me wanted.” Zagore’s entry on to the Russian list of targets came after his colleague Olesia Krivtsova was sentenced in absentia in July to six years in a penal colony on charges of “justifying terrorism” and “discrediting” the Russian army. Last year, the paper’s news editor, Farida Kurbangaleeva, was sentenced in absentia to eight years in prison for “spreading false information” about the Russian army and “justifying terrorism”. She had previously been labelled a “foreign agent” and an unsuccessful extradition request was made to the Czech Republic where she was living at the time. Another Barents Observer journalist, Georgii Chentemirov, has also been added to the “foreign agents” registry, criminally charged and fined. article.title: Russia and US seek to block plan for binding rules on autonomous weapons
article.full_text: Plans to fill a gap in the global governance of autonomous weapons are in jeopardy as a group of nations led by Russia and the US move to use a UN conference this month to block proposals to negotiate a legally binding set of rules. The scale of the opposition will become clear at a diplomatic retreat starting on Friday before the seventh review conference on “certain conventional weapons” in Geneva due to be attended by 128 countries from 16 to 20 November. The review conference is seen as the key moment when the world could decide whether to back a mandate to negotiate a legally binding instrument negotiated within a defined timetable. The speed with which autonomous weapons are being developed and used in warfare is widely acknowledged. Anna Hehir, the head of military AI governance at the Future of Life Institute, an independent nonprofit, said: “States have never been closer to launching a global agreement on AI weapons. A lot of the hard work has already been done and states have now agreed by consensus to elements of a draft treaty text that would be the basis for negotiations to start. “But we will likely see some states hide behind language that has the veneer of progress but advocates for a continuation of endless discussions on voluntary measures that have no teeth. The proposals for more years of discussions on non-legally binding measures are smokescreens to keep autonomous weapons systems unregulated and states unaccountable for their use.” Discussions have been under way on the issue inside the UN for nearly three years but Russia, the US and Israel, among others, are pushing against the review conference setting a timetable for a legally binding instrument. In an intervention timed to influence the review conference, Pope Leo XIV stressed that decisions relating to human life could never be given to machines. He said: “Decisions affecting human life, freedom and the use of force must always remain subject to effective, informed and responsible human oversight. For this reason, artificial intelligence must be ‘disarmed’, and I encourage the states meeting in Geneva in November to take concrete steps toward banning lethal autonomous weapons.” Human Rights Watch and the campaign group Stop Killer Robots argue that weapons systems, assisted by AI, are proven to behave unpredictably, increasing the risk of fatal errors and battlefields spinning out of human control. The International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) said on Thursday: “The time has come to move from discussion to negotiation on new international rules to regulate autonomous systems. The world cannot afford further delays.” In July, Ukraine reported for the first time that Russia had used an AI-guided drone, which struck a propane tank at a fuel station in Zaporizhzhia. The Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy, has warned about the speed of AI weapon development, calling for the Ukraine war to be ended before AI takes over the battlefield. On 22 October, a coalition of 50 states including Ireland, Italy, Brazil, Mexico, France and Germany called for the conference to agree a strict negotiating mandate. The ICRC separately reported that more than 70 states supported beginning negotiations on a legal instrument. The UK did not back the Irish statement and has previously argued that existing international humanitarian law is sufficient basis for the regulation of such weapons. The Ireland-led group proposed a mandate to be agreed by the review conference that would establish a time-limited expert group tasked with negotiating the needed rules over three sessions in Geneva in 2027, totalling 25 days. The group would be required to submit a report containing the draft protocol to that year’s annual meeting, expected to take place later in 2027.
